items.title: “我们可能正在寻找张力”：formafantasma 谈展览空间设计
items.desc: 从白色立方体到纸板隔板，设计工作室的设计师研究建筑如何塑造我们所看到的，我们如何移动，以及艺术品如何相互关联。
items.articleText: formafantasma on research, design, and the exhibition space For Formafantasma , the Milan- and Rotterdam-based studio founded by Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin, exhibition design starts with looking closely at the relationship between the artworks, the building, the institution, and the people moving through it. The duo’s research-driven practice often looks at materials, culture, and the relationship between tradition and contemporary production, and they bring the same curiosity to exhibition-making. They look for what they call ‘the tension’ in a project — the moments when the artworks, architecture, curatorial idea, and established ways of displaying art don’t quite line up. ‘There is no fixed methodology, because exhibition design is always relational,’ Formafantasma tells designboom . Research and design happen at the same time in the duo’s process. The studio looks at the artworks, their material and historical context, the building they will be shown in, and the conventions of display, while also testing walls, materials, sightlines, and other ways of organizing the space. Sometimes, a seemingly pragmatic decision can reveal the larger question. ‘An apparently pragmatic decision, a wall, a fabric, a particular sightline, reveals a conceptual question that becomes central to the project,’ they explain. The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Bernhard Strauss, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum challenging the supposedly neutral exhibition space That way of working also leads Formafantasma to question one of the most familiar conventions of contemporary exhibition-making: neutrality. The white cube can appear to disappear around an artwork, but the studio argues that its familiarity does not make it neutral. ‘A white plaster wall is no less designed than a metal or textile wall,’ they tell us. ‘It has simply become so familiar within contemporary art that we have stopped seeing it as a choice.’ Their exhibitions of Caravaggio and Bernini at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam and Mike Kelley at Moderna Museet show how they approach this idea differently depending on the work. For Caravaggio and Bernini, they moved away from the darkness and theatrical lighting associated with the artists, using an exhibition language closer to the white cube. With Mike Kelley, they did almost the opposite, bringing the industrial character of the museum into the foreground through metal panels. In both cases, the architecture around the works is treated as part of the exhibition and not as something that fades into the background. ‘The response therefore cannot precede the question,’ Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin explain . ‘It emerges from looking very closely at what is already there.’ For the studio, the objective is to identify the particular spatial conditions that might make relationships within each project more visible or more complicated. ‘We are less interested in finding a visual language that will unify everything than in understanding what spatial condition might make the relationships within an exhibition more legible or more complex,’ the duo shares with designboom. This also explains their interest in the history of display itself. The way objects are exhibited is never simply a technical matter. ‘We have become increasingly interested in the exhibition itself as an object of inquiry: why a wall looks the way it does, why information occupies a particular position, why visitors are expected to move or sit in particular ways, why some materials appear neutral while others become immediately visible,’ they add. The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Bernhard Strauss, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum turning curatorial ideas into spatial conditions This relationship between concept and physical space is evident in Formafantasma’s work for the 2026 Diriyah Contemporary Art Biennale. Curators Nora Razian and Sabih Ahmed were thinking about movement, migration, oral transmission, and different forms of passage. The Biennale’s setting in the JAX district, meanwhile, consisted of very large industrial spaces. Formafantasma introduced porous textile partitions and wooden structures that established boundaries without severing one space from another. Visitors could often perceive another work, room, or presence through the architecture. ‘The curatorial idea of movement therefore wasn’t represented symbolically; it began to affect how boundaries themselves behaved,’ the studio highlights. Instead of translating a curatorial idea into an obvious visual metaphor, Formafantasma allows it to influence the physical organization of the exhibition. The conceptual and the practical develop alongside one another, a process that applies to questions that might initially appear purely technical, such as whether a work can tolerate daylight, how much acoustic separation a sound work requires, what should be visible behind an artwork, where visitors can rest, and how much material should be introduced for an exhibition that will exist for only a few months. ‘Conceptual questions and technical questions are not separate for us,’ they say. ‘The exhibition emerges through their negotiation.’ The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Martin Schgaguler, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum providing structure without prescribing interpretation Visitor movement is another area where Formafantasma resists the idea of complete control. Sightlines, thresholds, concealment, and revelation can all affect what becomes visible and when, but the studio is wary of treating an exhibition as a choreography in which every visitor follows an intended sequence. ‘We would resist thinking of movement as something we can completely choreograph,’ they explain. ‘Choreography can imply that the designer knows how the visitor should move and what they should experience at each moment. items.articleText: California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times . The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers, while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems. Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. items.title: 下载：调查美国边境“虚​​拟墙”的死亡事件
items.desc: 这是今天的The Download版本，我们的工作日时事通讯，提供有关技术世界每日发生的事情的信息。美国在边境监控上花费了数十亿美元
items.articleText: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die? When José Morales Bernal crossed the border into the US in April 2024, the day before his 32nd birthday, he was within range of three surveillance towers equipped with cameras and AI to automatically detect and track people. If the system worked as intended, Morales should have been apprehended. If he needed medical help, agents were trained to provide it. None of that happened. Instead, Morales died just 360 feet from the closest tower. It was local landfill workers, rather than Border Patrol, who first spotted him. An autopsy concluded that he had died of “environmental exposure.” A first-of-its-kind investigation by MIT Technology Review reveals that deaths like Morales’s are startlingly common. After mapping nearly 4,000 locations where human remains were found against information on nearly 600 surveillance towers, we discovered that a humanitarian crisis at the border has unfolded in view of the government’s own cameras. Read our full investigation into the deadly failings of the virtual wall . —James O’Donnell and Eileen Guo Learn more: As part of our 15-month investigation, we created the first comprehensive map of deaths near US-Mexico border surveillance towers. Take a look at that map , and read about how we made it . The US government is about to spend another $1 billion to triple the virtual wall’s size, yet we found it has systemic flaws: broken towers, algorithms that failed to detect people and agents who simply did not respond to alerts. Here are four ideas for what Customs and Border Protection should do to rectify those failures. An analysis by the Times of San Diego found at least 138 cases since 2022 in which migrants’ remains were found within the nominal range of a nearby surveillance tower. A separate MIT Technology Review analysis estimated that more than half of those people were likely within a tower’s field of view. Gómez Hernández was one of them. Here’s her story, written by our partners at Times of San Diego . All of these stories are part of Dying on Camera , our new series investigating the failures of border surveillance technology and their human cost. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 An AI hallucination nearly triggered a US military operation A false report prompted plans to intercept a Chinese vessel. ( CNN ) + The incident comes as the Pentagon accelerates its use of AI. ( Ars Technica ) + “Humans in the loop” in AI war is an illusion. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Gemini has carried out Google’s first known autonomous AI hack Google says the behavior wasn’t “misaligned” because its safety measures caught it. ( WSJ $) + Here’s why AI agents cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The US has proposed an AI safety alert system with China It would flag AI incidents that pose national security risks. ( AP ) + Trump and Xi will consider the proposal at their summit this week. ( NBC News ) + Could AI really kill us all? ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 California’s governor has ordered work on an AI “kill switch” It’s part of Gavin Newsom’s executive order on AI safety. ( NBC News ) + The order also calls for independent oversight of AI companies. ( NYT $) 5 Data centers are turning to forever chemicals for cooling PFAS cooling can reduce water use but raises pollution risks. ( Fortune ) + US regulators are fast-tracking PFAS for data center cooling . ( The Hill ) 6 Iran and China used AI agents to automate influence campaigns The agents created fake accounts and posts with little human input.( NYT $) + AI persuasion has entered elections. ( MIT Technology Review ) 7 Trump wants a new AI czar and an “AI Force” modeled on Space Force But he hasn’t said what the new force would do or where it would sit. ( Axios ) + The tech industry is scratching its head over the proposal. ( Politico ) 8 A cybercrime feud has erupted after a group hijacked a rival dark website The notorious ShinyHunters says it took control of cl0p’s site. ( Reuters $) 9 Gambling giant DraftKings used AI to target “profitable losers” The model scored users on how they responded to promotions. ( NYT $) 10 SpaceX’s next Starship flight will attempt its first orbital mission It will also deploy working Starlink V3 satellites. ( New Scientist $) Quote of the day “There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world.” —Nvidia’s Jensen Huang dismisses warnings that AI could wipe out humanity by 2030 in an interview with CBS News . One more thing AI is pushing the limits of the physical world Architecture often assumes a binary between built projects and theoretical ones. What physics allows in actual buildings is vastly different from what architects can imagine and design. But the latest advancements in AI have prompted a surge in the theoretical. That shift was on display at an exhibition at Brooklyn’s Pratt Institute, which brought together works from more than 30 practitioners exploring AI’s experimental, generative and collaborative potential to open up new areas of architectural inquiry. See how architects and designers are using AI to imagine what could be built . —Allison Arieff We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A beautiful new cat species is the first to be discovered in a century. + Explore Floor796, a massive, interactive pixel art pop-culture megastructure . + The HTML Review is an annual journal of literature made for the web that offers a refreshing, creative take on what online publishing can be. + Discover how William Blake shattered the boundaries between poetry, painting, and printmaking—and why the art world couldn’t understand him .

items.title: 艾略特·马奇 (Elliot March) 让风景引领道路
items.desc: MAWD联合创始人着眼于景观、建筑和房源的特色，塑造有归属感的空间
items.articleText: When Elliot March was a student at the University of Edinburgh, a chance meeting led to a successful partnership. “James White and I were late to the same class,” he says. “We immediately connected over a shared curiosity about architecture and design.” Early in their careers, both men worked at larger practices, continuing to learn and refine their craft. White became increasingly drawn to interiors and exploring how they shape an individual’s experience. Eventually, the pair branched out and established MAWD | March and White Design in 2010. The two friends treasured this newfound freedom to think more holistically about projects and develop their own point of view. March has led MAWD’s evolution from a luxury British interior design firm to the globally recognized practice it is today. The team has completed a range of projects across sectors, from hospitality to residential to yachts. No matter the size or scale of a room, March is less interested in arriving with a particular look in mind. “I’d rather let the architecture, location, light, materials, and daily life of a space lead us somewhere,” he says. “When all of those things come together naturally, the result feels like it belongs there.” Today, Elliot March joins us for Friday Five ! Here, he shares five locations that inspire him and five projects that reflect his work. Elliot March’s Inspirations Photography courtesy of Elliot March 1. Wynwood Walls I’ve been spending a lot more time in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood through my work on The Cloud One Hotel & Residences Wynwood , and it always gives me something new to look at. I love the energy of the murals against the area’s industrial backdrop and the constant tension between raw materials and expression. That contrast has stayed with me as we’ve thought about how the project can feel connected to Wynwood rather than simply placed within it. Photography courtesy of Elliot March 2. Paso Robles Wineries I’m drawn to the wineries around Paso Robles, California, for their relationship with the landscape and how architecture can feel quiet within it. The local stone, timber, concrete, and weathered materials have a particular quality that feels both grounded and tactile. I also love the way the buildings frame the surrounding vineyards rather than competing with them. It’s a landscape where material, light, and nature do much of the work. Photography courtesy of Elliot March 3. Yucca Valley Cycling through Yucca Valley, California, around sunset is one of my favorite ways to clear my head. The landscape changes so quickly at that hour. The colors get warmer, the shadows stretch out, and suddenly things you’ve passed a hundred times look completely different. I love that reminder to slow down and really look. Some of the best ideas come from noticing what is already there. Photography courtesy of Elliot March 4. Parte Vieja I love wandering through the Parte Vieja quarter in San Sebastián, Spain, because the details have so much character. The worn stone, painted façades, balconies, timber, tiled thresholds, and layers of history all sit together without feeling overly considered. It’s the kind of environment where you can spend an afternoon simply looking up and noticing things. I’m always interested in places that have developed organically over time, where the imperfections and traces of use are part of what makes them beautiful. Photography courtesy of Elliot March 5. Taos Pueblo I find the Taos Pueblo historic site in New Mexico incredibly moving. There’s a directness to the architecture found in the local materials and simple forms, and an unmistakable relationship to the landscape gives it so much warmth and presence. Nothing feels arbitrary. It’s a place that reminds me how meaningful architecture can be when it grows out of its environment, its materials, and the people who have shaped it over time. 5 MAWD Projects Photography by VMI Studio 1. The Cloud One Hotel & Residences Wynwood The Cloud One Hotel & Residences Wynwood is meaningful to me because of how much inspiration we have been able to draw from Wynwood itself. I’ve always been interested in neighborhoods where different histories and influences sit side by side, and Wynwood has that in abundance, from its warehouse and garment-district past to the art and creative energy that define it today. We wanted to capture some of that character through exposed concrete, wild oak, bronze, lush planting, and art curated by Goldman Global Arts , while still creating a place that feels calm and comfortable. I love that balance between the energy outside and the sense of retreat within. Photography by Evan Joseph 2. The Greenwich by Rafael Viñoly The Greenwich in Manhattan’s Financial District is especially personal to me. The late architect Rafael Viñoly invited MAWD to lead the interiors, prompting my move from London to New York and, shortly after, the opening of our New York headquarters. It also gave us the chance to bring our superyacht design experience into a Manhattan residential setting. The bookmatched Noir Saint Laurent marble behind the front desk, with its subtle nautical quality, is one example. I love that the project represents both a new creative chapter for MAWD and a pivotal one for me personally. Photography courtesy of Strategic Property Partners 3. Water Street Tampa What draws me to the forthcoming residences at Water Street Tampa is the relationship between the architecture and the way people live there. Tampa has this wonderful indoor-outdoor rhythm, so we started by looking at the building’s portals, louvers, and courtyards and thinking about how some of that language could carry through to the interiors. The light and tropical landscape gave us permission to be a little more expressive with color and material. I love projects where the location pushes you somewhere you might not have gone otherwise, and this has been one of those. Photography courtesy of Related Ross 4. Edgeworth What excites me
